Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

I'm Professor, I'm in the Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering.

Key details

  • Today, we're going to learn the ideal and practical diode characteristics along with the diode resistances.
  • As we see from the diagram, we're going to learn about the equivalent representation of the diode, this has been written based on the characteristics curve.
  • There are two types of practical diodes out there.
  • There are two types of diodes representations are there.
  • One is ideal diode.
  • When an ideal diode is forward biased, as shown in the diagram here, it offers no resistance and act like a closed switch.
  • Likewise, the ideal diode under reverse bias offers infinite resistance, hence it is a open switch.
  • Coming to the practical diode as shown, the diode which is said to be forward biased, it starts conducting at a new voltage, which is 0.7 for silicon and reverse bias, no current, and this practical diode is considered as, again, the open switch, similar to that of an ideal diode.
  • For germanium, it would be 0.3.
  • So the next point, what we are going to understand is diode resistances.
  • An actual diode offers a very small resistance, non-zero, when forward biased, and is called the forward resistance.
  • Whereas it offers very high resistance, not infinite, when reverse biased, and is also called as a reverse resistance.
  • Type of applied voltage or a signal will define the following resistance levels.
  • Coming to the first DC or a static resistance, the application of an DC voltage to a circuit containing a semiconductor diode will result in operating point on a semiconductor diode characteristics curve, which is x-axis is VD, y-axis is.
  • Typically, the DC resistance of a diode is for forward bias, 10 ohm to 80 ohm.
  • Reverse bias, 10 megaohm.
  • Coming to the AC or a dynamic resistances, the application of a small AC voltage to a circuit containing a semiconductor diode offers AC resistance.
  • A straight line drawn tangent to the curve through Q point will define a particular change in voltage and a current.
  • That change in the voltage and change in the current determine the AC or a dynamic resistance, which is shown that is RD is equal to delta VD by ID for this region of the diode characteristics.
  • Coming to AC or a dynamic resistance, dynamic resistance can be found simply by substituting the quotient value of the diode current into the equation as RD is equal to 26 millivolts by ID, or RD dash is equal to 26 millivolts by ID plus.
  • This RB is the bulk current body resistances.
  • Typically, the AC resistance of diode in active region will range from 1 ohm to 100 ohm.
  • Further, the average AC resistance can also be calculated with a diagrammatic from the diode characteristics as shown.
  • If the applied input voltage is sufficiently large to produce a broad swing and a resistance determined by the straight line drawn between the two intersection established by a maximum and a minimum value of the input voltage is called the average AC resistance.
  • That is, RAV is equal to delta VD by delta V at point to point.
  • Then average AC, defined by the straight line between the limits of the operation.
